extracted.intended_audience: researchers (including graduate students and early-career scholars) interested in preprints and peer review practices
extracted.subtask_description: A university library guide summarizing models, benefits, risks, and practical tips for using preprints and participating in peer review (including getting credit and sharing non-article research outputs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invited reviewers (post-publication review model)
rubrics_metrics.description: An editor invites experts to comment on the published article. Once that work passes review, it is identified as a 'peer reviewed' publication and indexed within scholarly databases as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: F1000 Research, Copernicus. Use when an editorially-invited expert assessment and formal identification as peer reviewed is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volunteer reviewers (post-publication review model)
rubrics_metrics.description: A group of scholars are vetted by a journal and anyone from that group can review any published work. Each publication will determine if and how a review impacts the status of a work, and when it has been reviewed and edited enough to become 'peer reviewed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ScienceOpen, The Winnower. Understand the journal's specific rules about how volunteer reviews affect a paper's 'peer reviewed' status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open comments (post-publication review model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments and review happen on the article’s page, on blogs or other third-party sites. These comments can be made anonymously, pseudonymously, or with real names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This type of review typically won’t change the manuscript's status to 'peer reviewed', but can identify issues or surface interesting and high-impact articles. Examples: PubPeer, PubMed Commons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer review (transparency criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: In an open peer review model all aspects of the publication and review processes are made publicly accessible, including: the original manuscript, the names and full reports of all referees, any revised versions of the manuscript, and a list of all the amendments made by the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Wellcome Open Research. Use open peer review when maximum transparency of review process and provenance (who reviewed, what was changed) is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faster and wider dissemination (benefit of preprints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints enable faster and wider dissemination: no wait times, no paywalls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for rapidly sharing results and increasing accessibility; consider for time-sensitive findings or when broad access is a priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record of priority (benefit of preprints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints provide a record of priority via a permanent datestamp within ~24 hours of posting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuable for establishing precedence of results or ideas; cite the preprint date when claiming priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does not preclude publication (preprint policy consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Posting a preprint usually is not considered prior publication and does not preclude later journal publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always check specific journal policies (e.g., SHERPA/RoMEO) because some journals have different stances on preprints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of embargo violations (con of preprints / policy hazard)
rubrics_metrics.description: If press or public publish findings from a preprint, it may be considered prior publication and risk violating embargoes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious with press releases or public communications tied to preprints; verify funder/journal embargo policies before broad publicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing a body of work (benefit for career/funding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints can help establish a body of work; good for early career researchers. Some funders (e.g., NIH and Wellcome) accept preprints as part of applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use preprints to demonstrate productivity and ongoing work for job/funding applications, but follow funder and institutional guidance on citing/preparing preprints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid evaluation of results (benefit of preprints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints invite many readers ('lots of eyes') which can lead to rapid evaluation of results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage community feedback on preprints to improve manuscripts prior to journal submission; consider posting preprints to gather early critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of low quality (con of preprints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints may be perceived as low quality due to misunderstanding them as manuscripts that can't pass peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sharing preprints, clarify their status and whether they have undergone any formal review; be prepared to address misconceptions with readers or media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of disseminating invalid findings (con of preprints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unvetted papers may be picked up by the public, journalists, etc., risking dissemination of invalid or unreliable findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overstating preliminary results in preprints; include clear limitations and encourage cautious interpretation, especially for sensitive or high-impact topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get credit for peer review (track and verify reviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a Publons account to track and verify your peer review activities; connect Publons to ORCID to make review activities available to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these services to document reviewing work for CVs, promotion, funders, and scholarly profiles. Ensure privacy and journal policies permit listing reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share non-article research outputs (beyond the article)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research outputs other than articles are increasingly considered first-class: Data (DataCite, FigShare, disciplinary repositories), Code (GitHub, FigShare, Zenodo), Protocols (Open Science Framework).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deposit data, code, and protocols in appropriate repositories with persistent identifiers to increase transparency, reproducibility, and measurable impact.
